CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue active negotiations with the US and be prepared to commit to substantially increased purchases of US goods (soybeans, LNG, agriculture), while resisting binding structural reforms that would undermine industrial policy autonomy. Use the remaining time before the March 2 deadline to lock in a purchases-based deal that prevents tariff escalation from 10% to 25% on List 3. The Huawei/Meng Wanzhou situation should be compartmentalized from trade talks — do not let it derail negotiations, but do not formally concede the point.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: China faces a high and rising threat. Manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in December 2018 — first time below 50 since mid-2016 (Reuters, 2018-12-31). New export orders have contracted for seven straight months (sub-index at 46.6). Growth slowed to 6.5% in Q3 2018, the weakest since the global financial crisis, and independent forecasters expect ~6% in 2019 — the lowest since 1990 (Washington Post, 2019-01-07). US tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1, 2, and 3 at 10%), with a scheduled hike to 25% on $200B if no deal by March 2. The Huawei CFO arrest on December 1 adds a volatile non-tariff dimension — it has inflamed nationalist sentiment domestically, making any concession appear like capitulation, while the detention of two Canadians in retaliation risks further escalation. However, there are mitigating factors: the January 7-9 Beijing talks were extended to an unscheduled third day with constructive signals (Trump tweeted 'going very well'), China approved five GM crop imports as a goodwill gesture, soybean purchases resumed, and a draft foreign investment law addressing forced tech transfer was released. The services PMI remains above 50 at 53.8, cushioning the manufacturing contraction. China's $3T+ in FX reserves and policy tools (RRR cuts, fiscal stimulus) provide buffers, but deeper structural reform demands — IP enforcement, subsidy reduction, industrial policy constraints — represent existential risks to the CCP's growth model that cannot be conceded. The optimal action is to negotiate actively: offer substantial purchase commitments (which address the bilateral deficit without structural damage) while the 90-day window is open, buying time and preventing the tariff hike. This is not capitulation — it is pragmatic de-escalation under genuine economic duress.
key_factors: Manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in Dec 2018, first time below 50 since mid-2016
New export orders contracted for 7 straight months (sub-index 46.6)
US tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese imports; scheduled hike to 25% on $200B by March 2 deadline
Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou arrested Dec 1; two Canadians detained in retaliation; nationalist pressure limits concession space
Jan 7-9 Beijing talks extended to 3 days, described as constructive; progress on purchases but not on structural reforms
China approved GM crop imports and resumed soybean purchases as goodwill gestures
Growth expected to fall to ~6% in 2019, lowest since 1990
Services PMI still expansionary at 53.8, providing some cushion
China has $3T+ FX reserves and policy tools but faces debt/financial stability constraints

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5-10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest).
Trade talks resume in Beijing (working / mid-level). China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
Official PMI fell to 49.4 in December, below the 50-point level. New export orders shrank for a seventh straight month, sub-index falling to 46.6.
Talks extended for unscheduled third day. Progress on purchases of US farm and energy commodities. Structural reforms remain a sticking point.

Most independent economists expect China's growth rate to fall to about 6 percent this year, the lowest since 1990. Chinese are very eager to de-escalate because they're worried about domestic economic situation.
